newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica to abandon Cablevision venture - paper.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica to abandon Cablevision venture - paper.

text.p: Spanish telecommunications group Telefonica is to pull out of Cablevision, its joint venture with Spanish pay TV giant Sogecable, the daily El Mundo said on Saturday.
The decision comes just before the European Commission prepares to deliver the findings of its four-month investigation into the possible anti-competitive nature of the venture.
Telefonica sources said they had based their decision on the fear that Brussels would rule against the project, according to El Mundo.
The Commission could impose fines of more than 600 million pesetas on Cablevision it it found it guilty of abusing its dominant market position and of anti-competitive behaviour.

The joint venture was set up by Telefonica and Sogecable SA, a unit of Promotora de Informaciones SA (PRISA) and Canal Plus, in July 1995 to operate and distribute pay television and multimedia in Spain via cable TV networks.
The Commission started a full probe into the venture in July this year, saying it was a concentration with a European Union (EU) dimension which could go against EU competition rules.
The Telefonica sources said its directors would recommend the dissolution of Cablevision at the next board meeting due on November 11.
But they added that major Telefonica shareholder Banco Bilbao Vizcaya, which holds a 15.79 percent stake in Cablevision, would have to be consulted before the company was dissolved.

The Cablevision deal was reluctantly submitted to the Commission for clearance at the end of May, after the parent companies and the Spanish government denied for months that Brussels should deal with the case. They argued the operation had a Spanish, not a European, dimension.
The Commission has become increasingly tough on media deals, especially when they reflect what it sees as efforts by dominant companies to close the fast-growing pay-television market to competition.
Spain has some 10 million households with televisions, but only 200,000 have access to cable, making it one of the largest untapped markets left in western Europe.
